lessons.title: Windows Server Roles and What a Domain Controller Does

slots.practicalActivity: Download and install a free evaluation copy of Windows Server in VirtualBox or Hyper-V as your lab domain-controller-to-be, naming it LAB-DC01. From PowerShell, run Install-WindowsFeature -Name AD-Domain-Services -IncludeManagementTools to install the AD DS role, then confirm with Get-WindowsFeature AD-Domain-Services showing Installed. Don't promote it to a DC yet — just confirm the role installed cleanly, and write one sentence each describing what the DNS, DHCP, and File Server roles would add if also installed.
slots.deliverable: A running Windows Server evaluation VM (LAB-DC01) with the AD DS role installed and confirmed via Get-WindowsFeature, plus one written sentence each on what the DNS, DHCP, and File Server roles would add.

lessons.title: Active Directory Structure: Domains, Trees, Forests, and OUs

slots.practicalActivity: On LAB-DC01, promote it to the first domain controller of a new forest (Install-ADDSForest -DomainName "contoso.local" or the AD DS Configuration Wizard). Once it reboots and you can log in as the domain Administrator, open Active Directory Users and Computers (dsa.msc) and build the lesson's 4-level OU structure: a Corp OU and a Departments OU containing Sales, IT, HR, and Finance, each split into its own Users and Computers sub-OUs.
slots.deliverable: A promoted domain controller (contoso.local) and a real OU tree in Active Directory Users and Computers matching the Corp/Departments structure from the lesson, with at least 4 department OUs each split into Users and Computers sub-OUs.

lessons.title: Managing Users and Groups in Active Directory

slots.practicalActivity: In ADUC on your lab DC, right-click the Finance\Users OU and create a new user by hand. Then in PowerShell, run New-ADUser to create a second user and Add-ADGroupMember to add it to a new "Finance-Employees" global group, which you then nest inside a new "Finance-Share-RW" domain local group — the full A-G-DL-P pattern from the lesson. Confirm both users exist and the group nesting is correct with Get-ADGroupMember.
slots.deliverable: Two real AD users (one created via ADUC, one via New-ADUser), a Finance-Employees global group nested inside a Finance-Share-RW domain local group, confirmed with Get-ADGroupMember output showing correct nesting.

lessons.title: NTFS Permissions and Share Permissions

slots.practicalActivity: On LAB-DC01, create a folder C:\FinanceShare, share it over the network, and set its share permission for Finance-Employees to Change while setting the NTFS permission on the same folder to Read & Execute. Log on as (or runas) one of your Finance test users, connect to \\LAB-DC01\FinanceShare, and confirm you can open and run a file but cannot save a new one or delete anything — matching the lesson's "most restrictive wins" example exactly.
slots.deliverable: A real shared folder with a Change share permission and a Read & Execute NTFS permission set on it, with a logged-in test user's actual access (can open, cannot save or delete) confirming the most-restrictive-wins rule.

lessons.title: Group Policy Objects and How They Apply

slots.practicalActivity: On LAB-DC01, create a GPO called "Password Policy - Baseline" linked at the domain level setting minimum password length to 8, and a second GPO "Finance - Enhanced Password Policy" linked only to the Finance OU setting minimum length to 14. Run gpupdate /force and gpresult /r against a Finance-scoped object to confirm which policy actually won, then turn on Block Inheritance on the Finance OU, set the baseline GPO to Enforced, and re-run gpresult /r to confirm Enforced still reaches Finance despite the block.
slots.deliverable: Two real linked GPOs (a domain-level baseline and an OU-level enhanced policy) with gpresult /r output proving the OU policy wins by default, plus a second gpresult /r run showing an Enforced GPO overriding a Block Inheritance setting you turned on afterward.

lessons.title: Security Baselines and the CIS Benchmarks

slots.practicalActivity: Download Microsoft's Security Compliance Toolkit (SCT) for the Windows Server version you're running, and import its baseline GPO backup into Group Policy Management on LAB-DC01 using the Group Policy Management Console's Import Settings wizard. Link the resulting GPO to a test OU, then write a one-paragraph comparison of 3 specific settings in Microsoft's SCT baseline versus what you'd expect from a CIS Level 1 benchmark for the same OS, based on the lesson's description of each.
slots.deliverable: A real Microsoft SCT baseline GPO imported and linked to a test OU in your lab domain, plus a written one-paragraph comparison of 3 settings between the SCT baseline and a CIS Level 1 benchmark.

lessons.title: Windows Firewall and Windows Defender

slots.practicalActivity: On a domain-joined lab VM, open Windows Firewall with Advanced Security and create an inbound rule allowing file-sharing (port 445) for the Domain and Private profiles only, leaving Public at its default block — confirm the scope in the rule's Properties. Then run Get-MpComputerStatus and Get-MpPreference in PowerShell to confirm Defender's real-time protection and cloud-delivered protection are both enabled, noting which setting each cmdlet actually reports.
slots.deliverable: A real inbound firewall rule scoped to only the Domain and Private profiles (confirmed in the rule's Properties), plus actual Get-MpComputerStatus and Get-MpPreference output showing real-time and cloud-delivered protection status.

lessons.title: BitLocker and Data-at-Rest Protection

slots.practicalActivity: On a lab VM with a virtual TPM enabled in its VM settings, turn on BitLocker for the C: drive with manage-bde -on C: -RecoveryPassword. Confirm the 48-digit recovery key was generated, save it to a text file stored outside the encrypted drive, and run manage-bde -status C: to confirm the volume shows as fully encrypted and protected by the TPM.
slots.deliverable: A lab VM with BitLocker turned on for C:, a saved 48-digit recovery key stored outside the encrypted volume, and manage-bde -status output confirming full encryption and TPM protection.

lessons.title: Windows Event Viewer and the Security Log

slots.practicalActivity: On LAB-DC01, open Event Viewer via eventvwr.msc and browse the Application, Security, and System logs. Log out and back in as a standard, non-admin user and confirm you can still open Application and System but the Security log is inaccessible without elevation. Back as admin, use Filter Current Log on the Security log to narrow it down to just Event ID 4624 within the last 24 hours.
slots.deliverable: Confirmation (screenshot or written note) that a standard user cannot open the Security log while Application and System remain accessible, plus a filtered Security-log view showing only 4624 events from the last 24 hours.

lessons.title: Key Windows Event IDs Every Analyst Should Know

slots.practicalActivity: On LAB-DC01's Security log, log on and off a few times (locally and via RDP if you have a second machine) to generate real 4624 events with different Logon Type values, then deliberately fail a login 3 times to generate 4625s. Filter the log for 4624 and record each event's Logon Type (2, 3, or 10). Then create a new test user (4720) and add it to a security-enabled global group (4728), checking whether a 4672 follows if that account carries admin rights.
slots.deliverable: Real captured 4624 events showing at least 2 different Logon Type values, a burst of 4625 failures from a deliberate bad password, and a 4720-then-4728 sequence from creating and group-adding a test account, with a note on whether a 4672 followed.

lessons.title: Introduction to Sysmon for Deeper Visibility

slots.practicalActivity: Download Sysmon from the Microsoft Sysinternals site and a published baseline config (e.g. SwiftOnSecurity's), then install it on LAB-DC01 with sysmon64.exe -accepteula -i config.xml. Confirm it's running with sysmon64.exe -c, then open a PowerShell session with an encoded command (powershell -enc <base64>) to generate a Sysmon Event ID 1, and open a browser to generate an Event ID 3, checking both under Applications and Services Logs > Microsoft > Windows > Sysmon > Operational.
slots.deliverable: Sysmon installed and running with a real baseline config, plus a captured Event ID 1 (Process Create) showing a full command line and a captured Event ID 3 (Network Connection) showing a real source/destination IP and port.

lessons.title: Windows Audit Policy: What to Log and Why

slots.practicalActivity: On LAB-DC01, open secpol.msc and navigate to Advanced Audit Policy Configuration. Run auditpol /get /category:* to capture the current baseline, then enable Logon/Logoff, Account Management, and Privilege Use success-and-failure auditing with auditpol /set. Generate a few logons plus a new-user and group-membership change, then confirm the matching Event IDs (4624, 4720, 4728) now appear reliably in the Security log.
slots.deliverable: auditpol /get output captured before and after enabling the 3 key subcategories, plus confirmed Security-log entries for 4624, 4720, and 4728 generated after the policy change was applied.

lessons.title: sudo and the sudoers File in Depth

slots.practicalActivity: Set up a Linux lab VM for the rest of this course — a RHEL-family distro like Rocky Linux or AlmaLinux, since Chapter 5's SELinux content is RHEL-specific — in VirtualBox or a free cloud tier. On it, run sudo visudo and add a scoped rule granting a test user NOPASSWD access to exactly one absolute-path command (e.g. /usr/bin/systemctl restart sshd). Confirm the scoped command runs without a password prompt for that user while any other sudo command still prompts, then move the rule into its own file under /etc/sudoers.d/ and re-verify with sudo visudo -f.
slots.deliverable: A working RHEL-family Linux lab VM with a scoped sudoers rule in /etc/sudoers.d/ granting one test user NOPASSWD access to exactly one absolute-path command, confirmed working while other sudo commands still prompt.

lessons.title: PAM: Pluggable Authentication Modules Basics

slots.practicalActivity: On your lab VM, cat /etc/pam.d/sudo and /etc/pam.d/sshd to see which shared stack they include. Edit the system-auth stack to add pam_faillock.so with deny=5 unlock_time=900 in the preauth and authfail positions from the lesson, then deliberately fail a login 5 times in a row as your test user and confirm the account actually locks, checking status with faillock --user <user> and unlocking it early with faillock --user <user> --reset.
slots.deliverable: A real pam_faillock.so configuration added to your lab VM's auth stack, proven by a test user actually getting locked out after 5 failed attempts and unlocked early with faillock --reset.

lessons.title: Linux File Permissions Beyond the Basics: ACLs and the Sticky Bit

slots.practicalActivity: On your lab VM, create a file and run getfacl on it to see its base ACL. Use setfacl -m u:<seconduser>:r-- and setfacl -m g:<group>:rw- to grant a named user read-only and a named group read-write access without changing ownership, confirming the trailing + in ls -l and the mask:: entry in getfacl. Then create a world-writable scratch directory, chmod +t it, and have two different users create files in it, confirming one user cannot delete the other's file despite the shared write permission.
slots.deliverable: A file with a working ACL grant to a named user and a named group (confirmed with getfacl and the ls -l trailing +), plus a sticky-bit directory where one test user is proven unable to delete another's file.

lessons.title: Cron, systemd Timers, and Scheduled Task Security

slots.practicalActivity: On your lab VM, add a crontab -e entry that appends a timestamp to a log file every minute, confirm it's running by watching the log grow, then remove it and build the systemd-timer equivalent (paired .timer and .service units) using OnCalendar=, enable it with systemctl enable --now, and confirm with systemctl list-timers. Then create a deliberately world-writable script called from root's crontab, show its 777 permissions with ls -l, and fix it with chmod 750, writing one sentence explaining the privilege-escalation risk the original permissions created.
slots.deliverable: A working cron job and its systemd-timer equivalent, both proven to run on schedule, plus a demonstrated privilege-escalation risk (a 777 root-run script) found and fixed to 750 with a written explanation.

lessons.title: SELinux and AppArmor: Mandatory Access Control

slots.practicalActivity: On your RHEL-family lab VM, run getenforce and sestatus to confirm SELinux's current mode, then install httpd and run ls -Z on files in /var/www/html to see their security contexts. Switch to permissive mode with setenforce 0, deliberately move a file into the web root from a non-standard location so it gets the wrong context, confirm Apache can't serve it correctly once you flip to enforcing, then fix the context with restorecon -R, re-run setenforce 1, and confirm the file now serves correctly.
slots.deliverable: Real getenforce and sestatus output, a demonstrated SELinux denial caused by a mislabeled file under enforcing mode, and the same file fixed with restorecon and re-confirmed working under enforcing mode.

lessons.title: auditd and Linux System Auditing

slots.practicalActivity: On your lab VM, add a persistent watch rule in /etc/audit/rules.d/shadow.rules watching /etc/shadow for write and attribute-change access, tagged shadow_changes, then load it with augenrules --load (or restart auditd). Trigger a real change by running passwd on a test user, then run ausearch -k shadow_changes and aureport -au to confirm the event was captured with the correct timestamp, process, and user ID.
slots.deliverable: A persistent auditd watch rule on /etc/shadow confirmed loaded after a restart, plus real ausearch -k shadow_changes output showing a passwd-triggered change with its timestamp and user ID.

lessons.title: SSH Hardening Beyond Key-Based Auth

slots.practicalActivity: On your lab VM, with SSH key login already confirmed working, open a second session before touching anything. In the first session, edit /etc/ssh/sshd_config to set PermitRootLogin no, AllowUsers (your test username), and MaxAuthTries 3, run sshd -t to validate, then restart sshd. From a third, brand-new terminal, confirm you can still log in with your key before closing either of the first two sessions.
slots.deliverable: An sshd_config with root login disabled, an explicit AllowUsers list, and MaxAuthTries 3, validated with sshd -t and proven safe by a fresh third-session login succeeding before the original sessions were closed.

lessons.title: fail2ban and Brute-Force Protection

slots.practicalActivity: Install fail2ban on your lab VM, create /etc/fail2ban/jail.local with an [sshd] jail setting maxretry=5, findtime=10m, and bantime=1h, and enable it. From a second terminal, deliberately fail your own SSH login 5 times to trigger the threshold, then confirm with fail2ban-client status sshd that your own test IP actually got banned, and reverse it with fail2ban-client set sshd unbanip.
slots.deliverable: A working fail2ban sshd jail with real maxretry/findtime/bantime values, proven by an actual ban triggered by 5 failed logins and confirmed and reversed with fail2ban-client status and unbanip.

lessons.title: Patch Management Fundamentals and Patch Tuesday

slots.practicalActivity: Pick 3 real CVEs patched in the last 12 months for an OS or application you use, found on the vendor's own security advisory page, and for each one write a sentence estimating the exposure window between the patch's release and when most machines would realistically have installed it, based on the lesson's staged-rollout timeline. Then write a one-paragraph pilot-ring rollout plan for a fictional 200-server fleet, naming which machines go in the pilot ring and how long you'd wait before the broader rollout.
slots.deliverable: Written notes on 3 real recent CVEs with estimated exposure windows sourced from a vendor advisory, plus a one-paragraph staged-rollout plan (pilot ring plus wait time) for a fictional 200-server fleet.

lessons.title: WSUS and Windows Update for Business

slots.practicalActivity: If you have access to a Windows Server lab environment, install the WSUS role with Install-WindowsFeature UpdateServices -IncludeManagementTools, run the post-install configuration wizard, and create 2 computer groups ("Pilot Ring" and "Production") in the WSUS console. If a WSUS install isn't practical in your lab, instead write a one-paragraph decision memo for the lesson's 3,000-remote-laptop scenario, explicitly choosing WUfB over WSUS and naming specific deployment ring names and deferral periods.
slots.deliverable: Either a configured WSUS server with 2 real computer groups, or a written one-paragraph decision memo choosing WUfB for a remote fleet with specific ring names and deferral periods.

lessons.title: Linux Patch Management with apt and yum/dnf

slots.practicalActivity: On a Debian-family lab VM (or WSL), run sudo apt update followed by sudo apt upgrade and capture the real output of both. On your RHEL-family VM, run sudo dnf upgrade (or yum check-update then yum update) and compare its single-command workflow to apt's two-step process in writing. Then install and configure unattended-upgrades (Debian) or dnf-automatic (RHEL) to apply security-only updates, confirming the config file is actually scoped to security updates rather than everything.
slots.deliverable: Real apt update/upgrade output from a Debian-family system, real yum/dnf output from a RHEL-family system, and a working unattended-upgrades or dnf-automatic config confirmed scoped to security updates only.

lessons.title: Vulnerability Scanning Concepts and CVE/CVSS

slots.practicalActivity: Pick 3 real CVEs from a vendor advisory (Microsoft, Red Hat, or any software you use) and look up each one's real CVSS Base score and vector string. For each, identify the Attack Vector, Privileges Required, and resulting severity band (Low/Medium/High/Critical), then write a one-sentence prioritization judgment for each as if it applied to a fictional internet-facing server versus an isolated lab machine — same CVE, different environmental priority.
slots.deliverable: 3 real CVEs with their actual CVSS Base scores, vectors, and severity bands looked up from a vendor advisory, plus a written prioritization judgment for each under 2 different environmental scenarios.

lessons.title: Antivirus vs. EDR: How Endpoint Protection Has Evolved

slots.practicalActivity: On a Windows lab machine, run Get-MpThreatDetection to see what Defender's signature engine has caught historically. Then research one specific EDR product (CrowdStrike Falcon, SentinelOne, or Defender for Endpoint) on the vendor's own site and write a one-paragraph description of its process-tree feature, citing the actual capability name the vendor uses, explaining in your own words how it would have caught the lesson's fileless-phishing example when signature AV would not.
slots.deliverable: Real Get-MpThreatDetection output from a lab machine, plus a written paragraph naming one real EDR product's process-tree feature and explaining how it catches a fileless attack that signature AV misses.

lessons.title: Windows Defender for Endpoint Concepts

slots.practicalActivity: On a Windows lab machine, run Get-MpComputerStatus, Get-MpThreatDetection, and Get-MpPreference, and record exactly what each reports about real-time protection status, detected threats, and exclusion settings. Then research Microsoft's documentation on onboarding a device to Defender for Endpoint via Group Policy or Intune, and write out the exact sequence of steps you'd follow to onboard 500 machines at once rather than one at a time.
slots.deliverable: Real output from all 3 Get-Mp* cmdlets on a lab machine, plus a written step-by-step onboarding sequence (via GPO or Intune) for a 500-machine fleet, sourced from Microsoft's actual documentation.

lessons.title: Linux Endpoint Protection Options

slots.practicalActivity: On your Linux lab VM, install ClamAV, run freshclam to update its signature database, then clamscan -r against a real directory (e.g. /var/www or /home), confirming it completes and reports its scan results. Check systemctl status clamav-daemon to confirm the daemon runs continuously rather than depending on manual scans. Then research, on the vendor's own documentation, which telemetry source (auditd or eBPF) one real commercial Linux EDR agent (CrowdStrike Falcon, SentinelOne, or Defender for Endpoint's Linux sensor) actually uses.
slots.deliverable: A real clamscan run against a lab directory with freshclam-updated signatures, confirmed clamd running continuously via systemctl status, plus a researched, cited answer on which telemetry source one real commercial Linux EDR agent uses.

lessons.title: Asset Inventory and Why You Can't Protect What You Can't See

slots.practicalActivity: Run an nmap ping sweep (nmap -sn) against your own home or lab network's subnet to find every live device actually responding, then run nmap -sV -O against one of them to fingerprint its OS and running services. Compare the scan's results against your own mental list of what you expected to be on that network, and write down any device the scan found that you'd forgotten about or didn't expect — your own small-scale version of the CMDB-versus-discovery-scan gap from the lesson.
slots.deliverable: Real nmap -sn and nmap -sV -O output from your own network, plus a written comparison identifying at least one device the scan found that wasn't on your expected list.

lessons.title: Lab: Hardening a Windows Server Baseline

slots.practicalActivity: On LAB-DC01 (or a second domain-joined member server), run the lesson's full Windows hardening checklist end to end: confirm the CIS-based GPO baseline applied with gpresult /r, scope Windows Firewall inbound rules to the Domain profile only while leaving Private/Public at default deny, turn on BitLocker with manage-bde -on and back up the recovery key to AD with manage-bde -protectors -adbackup, enable the 3 key audit subcategories with auditpol /set, and install Sysmon with a baseline config, confirming all 3 event types are logging.
slots.deliverable: A fully hardened lab Windows server with verified GPO baseline application, scoped firewall rules, BitLocker enabled with an AD-escrowed recovery key, enabled audit subcategories, and running Sysmon — each step confirmed with its own command output.

lessons.title: Lab: Hardening a Linux Server Baseline

slots.practicalActivity: On your Linux lab VM, run the lesson's full hardening checklist: scope sudoers to one service account's single command plus requiretty/log_input/log_output Defaults, flip SELinux from permissive to enforcing only after checking ausearch -m avc -ts recent and running restorecon, harden sshd_config to key-only auth with AllowUsers and MaxAuthTries 3 paired with an active fail2ban jail, and add 3 persistent auditd watch rules on /etc/passwd, /etc/shadow, and /etc/sudoers tagged appropriately.
slots.deliverable: A fully hardened lab Linux server with scoped sudoers logging, SELinux confirmed enforcing after an AVC denial check, key-only SSH paired with an active fail2ban jail, and 3 persistent auditd watch rules — each verified with its own command output.

lessons.title: Case Study: Responding to a Failed Security Audit

slots.practicalActivity: Using your own lab environment, deliberately recreate one of the lesson's 3 audit findings — leave a server unpatched for a stretch, widen a GPO's local Administrators scope, or set PermitRootLogin yes on a Linux box — then remediate it following the lesson's exact remediation sequence (triage by CVSS score, re-check with Get-GPOReport, or disable root login and search auth logs for suspicious activity during the exposure window), documenting the before and after with real command output.
slots.deliverable: One deliberately recreated audit finding from your own lab environment, fully remediated following the lesson's sequence, with real before-and-after command output documenting the fix.

lessons.title: Chapter Capstone: OS Administration & Hardening Review

slots.practicalActivity: Write your own 90-day remediation plan modeled on the lesson's structure, naming the specific real commands and tools from this course (not generic descriptions) you'd run in each of the 4 weeks across your own lab's Windows and Linux machines. Then write a final resume bullet summarizing the concrete, hands-on hardening work you did across this entire course — GPOs linked, BitLocker enabled, SELinux enforced, SSH hardened, auditd rules written — naming specific tools, not vague claims.
slots.deliverable: A written, week-by-week 90-day remediation plan naming specific real commands and tools from this course, plus a resume bullet summarizing the hands-on hardening work completed, naming specific tools and techniques used.

monthlyMilestoneContribution: A student finishing this course can administer and harden a real mixed Windows/Linux environment end to end — standing up and promoting a Windows Server domain controller, structuring Active Directory into OUs with properly scoped security groups and NTFS/share permissions, authoring and linking GPOs (including CIS/SCT security baselines, Windows Firewall profiles, and BitLocker with AD-escrowed recovery keys), configuring Windows audit policy and Sysmon for real security-log and process-level visibility, and reading key Windows Event IDs like 4624/4625/4720/4728/4672 to recognize a credential-escalation pattern — while on the Linux side scoping sudoers and PAM lockout policy, managing ACLs and the sticky bit, securing cron and systemd timers against privilege escalation, enforcing SELinux/AppArmor mandatory access control, writing auditd watch rules, hardening SSH to key-only authentication, and deploying fail2ban — and has personally run both a Windows and a Linux server-hardening lab, triaged real CVE/CVSS-scored vulnerabilities, compared antivirus against EDR, run a network discovery scan against a real asset inventory, and walked through remediating a failed security audit across both operating systems.
